children: Iron ore prices rose slightly on Wednesday, reversing earlier losses, as investors shifted focus from demand prospects in top consumer China to possible stimulus measures from Beijing and supply cuts among some small-sized miners.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
closed daytime trade up 0.14% to 709 yuan ($105.73) a metric ton, after earlier hitting its weakest since August 21 at 704.5 yuan.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange was 0.27% higher at $95.7 a ton, as of 0721 GMT. It earlier touched its lowest since August 20 at $95.05.
A slew of official data on Tuesday showed sluggish Chinese consumption and a worsening investment slump, reinforcing concerns over deepening economic imbalances.
China's tepid economic growth in August increased the probability of additional fiscal stimulus in the fourth quarter, Jacqueline Rong, chief China economist at BNP Paribas, said in a note.
Helping ore recoup earlier losses was also supply reduction caused by thinner margins squeezed by rising freight rates.

Brazilian iron ore miner Itaminas planned to suspend partial production, cutting about 200,000 tons of supply, according to a company spokesperson, refusing to disclose further details, including reasons behind it.
However, downside pressure persisted, as deepening losses among steelmakers raised fears of steel output cuts, which will weigh on feedstock consumption.

The state-backed China Iron and Steel Association, along with 45 major steelmakers including China Baowu Steel Group, called on domestic steelmakers across the industry to firmly implement production controls to lower elevated steel inventory, according to a statement on its WeChat account on Tuesday.
"The loss-suffering among steelmakers was mainly caused by rising feedstock prices," said Bancy Bai, an analyst at consultancy Horizon Insights.
